Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Swainson’s Hawks: a remarkable return to California’s Central Valley Oct 19, 2026 Swainson’s Hawks are medium-to-large raptors renowned for their elegant flight and extraordinary migratory journeys. Each year, these hawks travel thousands of miles between their breeding grounds in the western United States and Canada and their wintering sites in Central and South America. California’s Central Valley is especially critical to their life cycle, with 95 percent of the state’s Swainson’s Hawks nesting there. Upon arrival in the Central Valley, Swainson’s Hawks select nest sites near grasslands or agricultural fields, which offer abundant prey and shelter. During the breeding season, their diet consists mainly of rodents, rabbits, reptiles, and small birds, which are essential for raising their young. Outside the breeding season, they adapt by feeding primarily on insects such as grasshoppers, demonstrating remarkable versatility. Symptoms of Hepatitis A For Everyone Oct. 27, 2026 Key points Most people who get hepatitis A have a mild, short-term illness. You can still spread hepatitis A virus (HAV) even if you don't have symptoms. Adults are more likely than children to have symptoms. Signs and symptoms Symptoms of hepatitis A can be different for different people. If you do have symptoms, they can appear anytime between 2–7 weeks after exposure. While some people can feel sick for as long as 6 months, most symptoms are gone within 2 months. For Health Care Providers Clinical Signs and Symptoms of Hepatitis A Symptoms of hepatitis A can include: Dark urine or clay-colored stools Diarrhea Feeling tired Fever Joint pain Loss of appetite Nausea, stomach pain, throwing up Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice) Not everyone will develop symptoms However, adults with hepatitis A are more likely than children to have symptoms. Close sz17900's Diary BetterIME - JOSM 中文输入法优化插件 Posted by sz17900 on 5 April 2026 in Chinese (China) (‪中文(中国大陆)‬) . [English] BetterIME is a JOSM plugin that automatically manages Chinese IME state based on focus context, preventing IME from intercepting keyboard shortcuts while editing the map. GitHub: https://github.com/nj-yzf/josm-BetterIME 问题背景 使用中文输入法编辑 OpenStreetMap 时，JOSM 的快捷键（如 S 选择、A 添加节点、W 提高路径精度等）经常被输入法拦截，导致快捷键失效。每次都要手动切换输入法，非常影响编辑效率。 为此我开发了 BetterIME 插件，让 JOSM 根据当前操作场景自动控制输入法状态。 功能介绍 插件将输入法控制分为三种场景： 自动切换至中文输入法： - 编辑 name、name:zh、name:zh-Hans、name:zh-Hant、alt_name、operator 标签时 - 打开 F3「搜索预设组合」对话框时 默认英文，可手动切换： - 其他文本输入框（如 Ctrl+F 查找、其他标签编辑等） 禁用输入法（快捷键正常工作）： - 地图视图、工具栏等非文本组件，Shift/Ctrl+Space 也无法意外切换至中文 此外，插件还释放了 Ctrl+Space 快捷键（JOSM 默认绑定为「搜索菜单项」），让它回归系统输入法切换功能。 首选项设置 通过 编辑 → 首选项 (F12) 打开 BetterIME 设置页，可以： 启用/禁用自动输入法切换（总开关） 启用/禁用 F3 搜索预设对话框中的中文输入法 启用/禁用基于标签键的自动检测 自定义触发中文输入法的标签键列表（支持添加、删除、重置） 所有设置即时生效，无需重启 JOSM。 安装方式 方式一：JOSM 内置插件管理器 1. 打开 编辑 → 首选项 → 插件 2. 搜索 BetterIME 3. 勾选启用，重启 JOSM 方式二：手动安装 1. 从 GitHub Releases 页面下载 BetterIME.jar： https://github.com/nj-yzf/josm-BetterIME/releases 2. 将 JAR 文件复制到 JOSM 插件目录（Windows: %APPDATA%\JOSM\plugins\） 3. 在 编辑 → 首选项 → 插件 中勾选启用，重启 JOSM 兼容性 JOSM 19555 及以上版本 Java 11 及以上 目前仅在 Windows 上测试过，macOS 和 Linux 上的输入法框架不同，可能无法正常工作，欢迎反馈测试结果 反馈 如果遇到问题或有功能建议，欢迎在 GitHub 提交 Issue： https://github.com/nj-yzf/josm-BetterIME/issues 许可证：GPL-2.0-or-later（与 JOSM 一致） Discussion Leave a comment Log in to leave a comment

pages.description: Whether carnivorous dinosaurs had lips has long been the stuff of paleo-debate. A new study finds evidence that flesh covered the predators’ teeth.
pages.text: T. rex had lips, upending its enduring pop culture image | National Geographic Premium SCIENCE ​ T. rex had lips, upending its enduring pop culture image Whether carnivorous dinosaurs had lips has long been the stuff of paleo-debate. A new study finds evidence that flesh covered the predators’ teeth. Tyrannosaurus rex and other carnivorous dinosaurs likely had soft tissue that covered their sharp teeth, as seen in this illustration. Lips would have kept their teeth moist and protected—and ready to attack prey. Illustration by Mark P. Witton By Riley Black Published March 30, 2023 • 6 min read The fearsome jaws of Tyrannosaurus are famous. In museum halls, paleo art, and even feature films such as Jurassic Park , the Cretaceous carnivore has traditionally been depicted with banana-size fangs and a sinister grin. But paleontologists have now discovered that the living animal did not have a sharp-toothed smirk— T. rex , as well as many other carnivorous dinosaurs, had lips. Reported today in Science , a multi-institution team of paleontologists propose that carnivorous dinosaurs like T. rex and Allosaurus had fleshy lips covering their teeth, much as modern-day lizards do. The hypothesis will likely alter both the public image of dinosaurs as well as how paleontologists study the ways these terrible lizards fed. pages.title: T. Rex Was a Cannibal, Bone Gashes Suggest | National Geographic
pages.description: The formidable Tyrannosaurus rex had nothing to fear—except possibly its own kind, gnawed fossil bones suggest.
pages.text: T. Rex Was a Cannibal, Bone Gashes Suggest | National Geographic Tooth gouges on this 65-million-year-old T. rex toe bone could have been made only by another T. rex. Diagram courtesy Nicholas Longrich, Yale University T. Rex Was a Cannibal, Bone Gashes Suggest Mighty predators may have attacked kin or scavenged corpses. By Brian Handwerk Published October 15, 2010 • 3 min read The formidable Tyrannosaurus rex likely had nothing to fear—except possibly its own kind, a new study suggests. Paleontologist Nick Longrich of Yale University was examining dinosaur bones found in Montana when he noticed large gouges in bones that had yet to be indentifiied. The gouges had to have been made by a large carnivore, he said, and when the mystery fossils were deposited 65 million years ago, T. rex was the only North American carnivore large and toothy enough to make such marks. But the seemingly routine find took a macabre turn when Longrich discovered one of the bitten bones belonged to a T. rex —making it apparent evidence of cannibalism. This toe bone "has giant theropod bite marks, and the only one there [at that time] was T. rex ," he said. "There was really no other conclusion I could come to." (Related: "Tiny T. rex Ancestors Achieved World Domination." ) Further analysis in several fossil collections turned up three more similarly bitten T. rex bones. Longrich and colleagues speculate the giant predators may have engaged in cannibalism with some regularity—but it's unknown whether the dinosaurs fought to the death or simply scavenged T. rex corpses. pages.text: Taiwan's Most Breathtaking Mountain Landscapes Skip to main content Sponsored Content by None Taiwan’s Most Breathtaking Mountain Landscapes From urban parks to the wilds surrounding Taiwan’s tallest peak, here are seven incredibly majestic mountain adventures Taiwan, dubbed by Portuguese explorers the "Ihla Formosa," or "Beautiful Island," is home to over 200 mountain peaks above 9,800 feet. From walking through d eep green pine forests filled with birdsong to watching the sun rise over a carpet of clouds, a trip to the mountains is one of the best ways to appreciate Taiwan's immense natural beauty and biodiversity. What's more, Taiwan's hiking trails cater to outdoor enthusiasts of all abilities and ages th anks to well-marked signs, a plethora of rural lodging options and easy-to-navigate transportation systems connecting national parks and scenic areas to city centers. Traveling between cities and trailheads takes just a couple of hours; at most, half a day. From urban parks to the wilds surrounding Taiwan's tallest peak, here are seven incredibly majestic mountain adventures. Yushan National Park Mount Yushan , also known as Mount Jade, is not only the tallest peak in Taiwan, but also the tallest peak in Northeast Asia. Close TaoEngine's Diary 【有时间就来写写枞阳的一些事情】关于康居路 Posted by TaoEngine on 15 July 2026 in Chinese (China) (‪中文(中国大陆)‬) . osm的小伙伴们大家好，今天我无意中发现了osm可以写日记然后放在自己的首页中。有的小伙伴分析地区编辑完完整度，有的教大家正确使用地图标签。虽然我注册有三年多了但是论辈分还是个小老弟😂，那我就写写我比较擅长的东西，欸要不我就写写有关家乡的一些事好了哈 关于康居路 枞阳县枞阳镇旗山社区邻近枞阳县人民医院、银塘花苑与银塘星城这三个区域中间有一条三级道路，道路有花坛阻拦，两条单行道形式，双向四车道（高峰期两车道因为两边可以停车） 这条道路的命名其实非常迷，枞阳县地图与天地图将其命名为健康路，而枞阳县ZY-02银塘行政区规划文件与地名信息系统将其命名为康居路（商业地图通常采用后者）。这条路到底叫康居路还是健康路？ 其实我住的地方离这条路不远，所以经常在傍晚散步时走这条路。根据我的见解以及查阅对应文件的思路，这条路现阶段应该还是命名为康居路为好，至少26年8月之前还是得叫它康居路 1. 根据路灯管理局的路灯标签判断 26年初，县里开展《城市生命线》安全设备部署工作，在大街小巷安装了监测设备，同时县里也提及同日设立路灯管理所。随即4月份县里的每个路灯都贴上了标签，其中这条路的路灯被贴上康居路标签。这项工作是领先于枞阳县地图的制作的，可以认定当前这条道路仍为康居路 2. 根据枞阳县ZY-02银塘行政区规划文件中康居小区存在与否判断 在枞阳县地图中，康居路并未消失而是跑到了旗山小学与中海山水城的区域中间，而它的命名依据是因为附近有个小区名为康居山庄。但是无论是在枞阳县ZY-02银塘行政区规划文件中，还是在旗山社区服务站点地图中，这个不是小区，是银塘村的回迁房，经简单查阅县政府公开文档初步确认区域名为银塘安置地。真正现存的“康居山庄”在妇幼保健院旁边，不过叫康居家园。当然不排除小区未来改名的情况 其次那条路虽然在路灯管理所的标签、附近停车场名称以及路牌中没有给出详细名称，但是在枞阳县ZY-02银塘行政区规划文件中，这条路被命名为安置地路。鉴于规划文件的审图号较枞阳县地图较新，该未分级道路我建议命名为安置地路，而保留原先的康居路命名位置 为啥要写这条路 上次有个过于热心的小伙伴将康居路所在道路标为健康路（与此同时他还把旗山路标为莲城路，而莲城路是天地图的一处过时标记，我有时间在下一次日记里说），希望我的笔记能在我没时间贡献枞阳的时候，给其他人一些有理可循的参考（与此同时我也会夹带一些私货介绍枞阳有什么有意思的地方，比如枞阳中学占据的地方曾经有个自然村叫答咀村，这个村的来历可神奇了，另开一个新坑），望大家多多关照👋 Location: 殷家老屋, 枞阳县, 枞阳镇, 枞阳县, 铜陵市, 安徽省, 246700, 中国 Discussion Comment from TaoEngine on 18 November 2026 at 04:59 打脸了，旗山小学那条路今天立牌子了😭就是康居路，马上改 Leave a comment Log in to leave a comment

Established by Congress in the Energy Policy Act of 2005, TCF invests millions of dollars each year to bridge the gap between research and commercial application. pages.text: Teesside conservationists search for European eels in River Tees Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Conservationists searching for large river eels 8 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Tom Burgess North East and Cumbria Tees Rivers Trust Tees Rivers Trust workers have been tagging eels to track their downstream migration Conservationists have spent summer and autumn searching for critically endangered eels to tag as they begin their downstream migration. The Tees Rivers Trust have found 12 large eels by fyke netting, a method of catching eels with a cylindrical net, around the River Tees catchment. The team managed to electronically tag 10 of them and the largest was 60cm (23ins) in length and weighted 435g (0.9lbs). Project manager Ellie Ward said the eels caught this year were not as large as usual and were "harder to catch". The team has been searching for "silver" eels which have finished maturing and are preparing to head back out to the Sargasso Sea near Bermuda. Ward said: "European eels start to migrate downstream during autumn and winter, when river discharges increase. "We suspect that low flows in summer that have continued into autumn have contributed to low catch rates so far this year." 'Mystery' species The Eels of Steel project is funded by Natural England and the Tees Rivers Trust has been conducting the research alongside Hull University. pages.text: Ten Turkey Facts to Gobble Up This Thanksgiving | Smithsonian Voices | National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute Smithsonian Magazine Skip to main content National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute Ten Turkey Facts to Gobble Up This Thanksgiving Dive into the juicy history of America’s favorite barnyard bird Mike Bock November 13, 2026 Get our Newsletter! Get our Newsletter! Like many birds, domestic turkeys, including this group at the Smithsonian's National Zoo in Washington, D.C., are social animals. Smithsonian/Brett Kuxhausen 1. Humans have been raising turkeys for thousands of years. Although indigenous peoples in North America have hunted wild turkeys since the end of the last Ice Age, the animals were first domesticated in Mexico around 2,000 years ago. Dinner wasn’t the original goal: archaeological evidence suggests turkeys were initially kept so their feathers could be used in clothing and ceremonial regalia. By A.D. 500, people were raising turkeys in what is now the United States too, judging by archaeological remains from caves in Arizona and New Mexico. Even so, those weren’t the birds that English settlers ate in the Thirteen Colonies. The domestic turkey descends from a southern Mexican bird that the Spanish took home in the 1500s. The birds then spread through Europe, and colonists brought them back across the Atlantic. The bird’s English name may reflect this long-distance trade: turkeys are thought to have reached England along winding trading routes that first passed through the country of Turkey. 2. pages.title: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms
pages.description: Scientists call the events permafrost detachment slides. Instead of thawing from the top down, these landslides seem to originate from a weakened base
pages.text: Thawing Permafrost May Have Created a New Type of Landslide, Which Could Become More Common as the World Warms Skip to main content A scar left by the 2018 Redstone River permafrost landslide, one of the two events investigated in the new study. Adapted from J. M. Young et al., Geophysical Research Letters , 2026 In 2017 and 2018, a pair of strange landslides moved huge masses of rock and dirt in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The events occurred in the central Mackenzie Valley, and one of them even dammed a river and created a lake . The two natural disasters are part of a new class of landslides scientists are calling “permafrost detachment slides” in a study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters in September. They may have been partially triggered by severe wildfires that occurred in 1995, which destabilized the ground and allowed the base of the permafrost to thaw. What’s more, these events may become more common as the planet continues to warm. “It’s a very dramatic manifestation of the changing climate,” says study co-author Joseph Young , a geoscientist who conducted the work at the University of Alberta in Canada, to Matt Simon at Grist . “They’ve only started happening in the last 10, 15 years, and it’s a very drastic and abrupt change in the landscape.” Young and his colleagues began the study after seeing something strange in the Northwest Territories in 2019. While conducting field research, they spotted large landslide scars in valleys that they knew were stable permafrost , or permanently frozen earth, reports Stephanie Pappas for Live Science

How do we separate facts from speculation? Recent claims from AI researchers have brought concerns about superintelligence into mainstream political debate. But how credible are these apocalyptic predictions? Are AI companies genuinely losing control of the technology? Or are these distracting us from harms already unfolding, including misinformation, cybercrime, job displacement and the concentration of corporate power? Join our wide-ranging panel of AI researchers, ethicists and policy experts as they examine where experts agree and disagree, interrogate the claims and counterclaims about the risks and calls to slow down its development, and explore crucial steps governments and tech companies must take now to help us safely navigate the AI revolution. Learn about other national symbols. History of the American flag The flag of the United States is a symbol of freedom before which Americans recite the pledge of allegiance . The flag's 13 red and white stripes represent the 13 original colonies. Its 50 white stars on a blue background represent the 50 states. Each of the colors on the flag has a meaning: Red: valor and bravery White: purity and innocence Blue: vigilance, perseverance, and justice A star is added to the flag when a new state joins the United States. The flag was last modified on July 4, 1960, when Hawaii was incorporated as a state. Learn more about the evolution of the American flag and its earlier designs. How to raise the flag Follow these guidelines to properly display the American flag [PDF, 162KB]. When to fly the flag at half-staff The American flag flies at half-staff or at half-mast when the country or a state is in mourning. The president, a state governor, or the mayor of the District of Columbia can order flags to fly at half-staff. In the foothills, access routes to the mines ran through an area called Nok. Over the years, with the exploitation of the mines and the local people who overwhelmingly provided the labor force, numerous fragments of ancient pottery came to light but were largely ignored. One piece, too striking to be disregarded, appeared in 1928: a small monkey head, sculpted in terra-cotta. The mine manager, Lt. Col. John Dent Young, had that piece and other fragments transferred to a museum in the city of Jos, the provincial capital. Enheduanna is often identified as the first author who appears independently in the historical record. Her hymns to the gods of Akkad and Sumer survived centuries after her death—and their translations are changing what modern scholars know about the role of women in the ancient Middle East. Source Photo for Illustration: Yale Peabody Museum By Liddy Berman Published September 8, 2026 More than 4,000 years ago, Enheduanna, high priestess of the Sumerian moon god and daughter of a king, labored over a palm-size clay tablet. Reed stylus in her hand, she pressed its tiny wedge-shaped tip into the clay to build the small, spiky characters of cuneiform. She had been driven from her temple home by a rebel leader who opposed her family’s imperial rule over the kingdoms of Ur and Uruk. Roman money, like this coin bearing the profile of Emperor Claudius, often contained silver, one of several precious metals that fueled Rome. A paragraph-long anecdote in the Annals by the Roman historian Tacitus, it tells a story found nowhere else, about an unpopular legate forcing legionaries into a treacherous mine at the frontier of the empire. It takes place during the reign of Claudius (A.D. 41–54), a time of furious expansion when Rome sought to swallow up the borderlands and their resources. The location mentioned in the Tacitus passage is vague, described as “in the district of Mattium,” just outside of Roman-occupied Germania Superior . The jacket is made of deer skin, stitched with deer skin cord and a bone awl, and adorned with moose teeth. The shirt underneath the jacket is made of undyed linen, hand stitched with linen thread. The skirt is made of deer skin and decorated with braided hemp strings. The continent of North America has been inhabited by humans for at least 16,500 years. As early as the 1500s, early settlers and European thinkers were interested in discovering how humans had come to populate North and South America. One theory suggested the migration of Norsemen across Greenland into North America. Another theory proposed the island of Atlantis as the origins of human life in the New World. Yet another idea proposed that the inhabitants had generated out of mud. However, by the early 1800s, scientists and theorists began discussing the possibility of a land bridge that had spanned between Asia and North America thousands of years ago. For all of human history people have looked up to the inky blackness of night and marvelled at the stars. Yet true darkness just isn’t something Europeans experience in the same way anymore due to artificial light illuminating the night sky. Light pollution can disrupt sleep and circadian rhythms, affect wildlife and ecosystems, and contribute to unnecessary energy use and carbon emissions. With this in mind, it’s no surprise more of us than ever are swapping chasing the sun for chasing the stars instead. DarkSky International is a non-profit organisation that certifies destinations around the world for the quality of their night skies, their approach to artificial lighting, conservation efforts and long-term commitment to protecting darkness. By Nicholas St. Fleur Published March 30, 2026 A newly discovered Spinosaurus sporting a bizarre, curved blade-like crest has snatched the headlines. But this massive carnivore is far from the only odd-looking prehistoric predator out there. In this episode of Dead World, our archaeology and paleontology video series, we look at some bizarre raptor-like dinosaurs that menaced the Mesozoic. These dinosaurs show just how strange evolution can get. Xenovenator , a recently discovered troodontid from Mexico, had a thickened skull that it may have used as a battering ram. Microraptor flew with four wings, and a study published in January shows how this dromeosaur used that extra pair to glide through the air unlike any bird today. A new, well-preserved specimen of Alnashetri cerropoliciensis from Argentina revealed that this chicken-sized dinosaur had unusually long arms compared to its alvarezsaur relatives. Knowable Magazine Whether it’s gushing from a bumped nose or pooling atop a pricked finger, our blood is some hue of red. But red-bloodedness isn’t universal in the animal kingdom. In some creatures, the vital fluid is purple; in others it’s yellow, green or even white. What imparts these different colors to the liquid of life? To find out, Knowable magazine waded into the research and spoke with a couple of scientists who have studied the stuff. Here’s what’s known about the science behind the hues. Bizarre blues and purples The rich red of vertebrate blood comes from hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells that contains iron atoms. Hemoglobin’s job is to deliver oxygen—and its iron atoms, which grab onto oxygen, make our blood look red. pages.text: The Complicated Social Life of a Tyrannosaurus Rex | National Geographic SCIENCE Why Everything We Thought We Knew About T. Rex is Getting … Messier Fossil evidence has shifted our view of T. rex from a complete loner tyrant into a more nuanced carnivore. Scarred skulls, scraped ground, and fossilized trackways suggest adult tyrannosaurs lived largely solitary lives, like modern big cats, but also gathered in communal display arenas to woo potential mates. GERD LUDWIG, National Geographic Image Collection By Riley Black Published October 8, 2026 Every time I’m in New York, I have to visit her. She’s always waiting in the same place, standing on the fourth floor of the American Museum of Natural History, grinning so wide that her teeth gleam under the bright lights. Experts know her as AMNH 5027. I know her as the first T yrannosaurus rex I ever met. Before the discovery of “Sue,” “Stan,” “Scotty,” and many other famous skeletons of Earth’s last great carnivorous dinosaur, AMNH 5027 was the icon. The partial skeleton was the first T . rex to include a complete skull – only slightly smushed. It left no doubt that the dinosaur was an impressive flesh-ripper, reconstructed with jaws agape when the museum’s paleontologists assembled real bones and casts in the world’s first great introduction to the dinosaur. (And, when Michael Crichton’s Jurassic Park needed a skeletal dinosaur for the cover, AMNH 5027 was the model.) By Nicholas St. Fleur Published July 27, 2026 Were Neanderthals Europe’s first painters? And did they use cave walls as their canvases? Scientists long thought that Homo sapiens —like us—were the only human species capable of creating artwork in caves. But in recent years, suspiciously old rock art found in caves throughout Spain, like the 65,000-year-old red lines in the Cave of La Pasiega , has led some to wonder if our extinct cousins were the artists instead. The findings left many experts wondering if our extinct cousins were the artists behind these prehistoric masterpieces. Now, researchers are hoping ancient DNA will hold the answer. pages.description: Paleontologists are resurrecting a famous Egyptian fossil site after a World War II air raid obliterated its most spectacular dinosaur discoveries—and their findings reveal a world even deadlier than expected.
pages.text: The Dinosaurs That Went Extinct ... Twice | National Geographic By Nicholas St. Fleur Published August 14, 2026 Stones & Bones is back! I’m Nicholas St. Fleur, a science editor at National Geographic, and today we explore the “lost dinosaurs” of the Bahariya Oasis in Egypt. Want to make sure you get every Stones & Bones newsletter? Enter your email here . To Egyptologists, the Bahariya Oasis is known as the Valley of Golden Mummies, a necropolis where archaeologists have uncovered hundreds of gilded and decorated mummies dating back to the Greco-Roman era, roughly 2,000 years ago. But to paleontologists, the oasis is sacred because of something far older and far more legendary: Spinosaurus . The first ever specimen of this ferocious river monster was collected here more than a hundred years ago, along with fossils of several other enigmatic dinosaurs. Until they were lost forever, casualties of the World War II bombing that destroyed much of Munich. Swallowed by the flames, these dinosaurs essentially went extinct twice. National Geographic Explorer Hesham Sallam , a paleontologist at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center in Egypt, has spent the past decade collecting clues to what the Bahariya Oasis looked like nearly 100 million years ago, long before it was buried beneath the desert. His team is still working to rebuild what was lost when the bombs obliterated the collection. SCIENCE LAELAPS The Echoes of Toothed Birds By Riley Black Published May 22, 2015 • 4 min read Whenever I spot a grebe, I try to imagine the bird with teeth. This is another symptom of a chronically fossiliferous mind. You see, these snake-necked swimming birds have traditionally been taken as a proxy for a specific sort of ancient avian called hesperornithiforms. Best known by, as you might guess, Hesperornis – these toothed birds pioneered the diving lifestyle between 113 and 66 million years ago. Today’s grebes and loons look like edentulous echos of these lost Cretaceous days, or, as beautifully expressed by ornithologist William Beebe : When in the depth of the winter, a full hundred miles from the nearest land, one sees a loon in the path of the steamer, listens to its weird, maniacal laughter, and sees it slowly sink downward through the green waters, it truly seems a hint of the bird-life of long-past ages. No surprise, then, that paleontologists past sometimes considered loons and grebes to be the descendants of Hesperornis . Their bones carry the same superficial similarity. But this is an evolutionary ruse known as convergence. Loons and grebes are copycats that independently took up the same lifestyle as the toothed birds that dove after fish in warm Cretaceous seas and sometimes wound up in the stomachs of monstrous marine reptiles. pages.text: The federal budget process | USAGov Skip to main content The federal budget process Learn about the federal government’s budget process. Steps include the president creating the budget plan and Congress’s work creating funding bills for the president to sign. Annual funding areas Every year, the U.S. Congress begins work on a federal budget for the next fiscal year. The federal government’s fiscal year runs from October 1 of one calendar year through September 30 of the next. And the annual budget covers three spending areas: Mandatory spending - funding for Social Security, Medicare, veterans benefits, and other spending required by law. This typically uses over half of all funding. Discretionary spending - federal agency funding. Congress sets funding levels for these each year. This usually accounts for around a third of all funding. Interest on the debt - this usually uses less than 10 percent of all funding. Creating the U.S. federal budget The budget planning begins a year before the budget is to go into effect. Federal agencies create budget requests and submit them to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB). OMB refers to the agencies’ requests as it develops the budget proposal for the president. The president submits the budget proposal to Congress early the next year. pages.text: The Global Web of Subsea Cables That Connects the World Can Now Detect Whales—Even When They're Silent Skip to main content A blue whale has been gathering food deep within the water column and reaches the surface with its throat pleats still distended, forming an enormous pouch. Within a few moments the whale will right itself up, expell the water, swallow the food, take several breaths and dive again. Francois Gohier/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Nearly 1,000 feet below the sea off the coast of Norway’s Svalbard archipelago, on a glass cable the width of a human hair, scientists detect a massive object moving through the water. It’s so big that the water it displaces when it moves produces low-frequency waves that radiate outward from its body. These waves ripple away toward the seafloor, where they stretch the tiny glass cable, buried beneath the seabed, almost imperceptibly. Onshore, laser pulses are fired down the cable, and as the light travels, microscopic imperfections scatter the light in the glass. Often, when researchers get feedback like this, it’s a submarine moving over the cable, or even a large ship chugging along the surface above. But today, they’ve found a blue whale. Typically, to find whales, scientists use a hydrophone, essentially an underwater microphone that can pick up a whale’s calls. They’re often fixed to the seabed or suspended from research vessels. Taking place at DEEP's saturation immersion diving facility in Tidenham, Gloucestershire, divers will live and work in pressurised chambers that replicate being 50m (164ft) underwater for up to a month. During that time the divers will plunge below the surface in a separate diving bell chamber for tasks such as inspecting pipes and welding, before slowly returning their bodies to normal surface pressure. DEEP dive manager Mark Hamilton said the company would now begin training the "next generation of saturation divers", which the industry "desperately needs". pages.text: The Grand Canyon is now a Dark Sky Park | National Geographic With low light pollution and new Dark Sky Park status, the Grand Canyon is one of the world's best places for stargazing. Photograph by Babek Tafreshi, Nat Geo Image Collection TRAVEL The Grand Canyon is now a Dark Sky Park—here’s why that matters The night skies over this American icon never looked brighter. By Nneka Okona Published June 20, 2019 • 5 min read It's been a big year for the Grand Canyon. The iconic park celebrates its centennial in 2019. Now it has received a new honor: International Dark Sky Park certification. The designation places the Grand Canyon into esteemed company with more than 60 dark sky parks, communities, and reserves in the United States. Only nine of the 61 national parks in the U.S. are certified by the International Dark Sky Association. These parks include Joshua Tree , Death Valley , and Big Bend National Parks . ( Discover more of the world's best stargazing destinations. ) Certification was a lengthy process for the Grand Canyon; preliminary efforts to meet the Dark Sky Park status began in 2016. A key initiative included outfitting the thousands of exterior lights in the park to decrease the amount of light pollution and enhance night sky star visibility. ( Our nights are getting brighter. Read more about the effects of light pollution.) The other half are trillions of microbes that thrive on or inside your body to form a group of biological communities known as the human microbiome. These microbial communities can vary greatly in size and character. The digestive tract hosts the largest number of microbes, forming a complex ecosystem known as the gut microbiome. Concentrated primarily in the large intestine, it consists of thousands of different species of bacteria, viruses, fungi and other microorganisms . Like a fingerprint, your gut microbiome is entirely unique. It starts developing the moment you are born. Over time, the amount and types of microorganisms change based on factors such as your environment and diet. Why is the gut microbiome important? We could not survive without these microscopic companions. Most share a symbiotic relationship with us, offering vital benefits while enjoying food and shelter in our body. Adam Steele/USFWS The mallard ( Anas platyrhynchos ) is a familiar inhabitant of North America’s waterways. In city parks, along wooded streams and across marshes, male mallards glide past with iridescent green heads and yellow bills, while mottled brown females disappear into the reeds. Few birds seem more ordinary, or more unmistakably wild. But beneath those familiar feathers lies a hidden history that toes the line between nature and domestication. For more than a century, captive-bred mallards have been released into North American wetlands, often to supplement populations for hunting. Over generations, those birds interbred with their wild counterparts, leaving behind a genetic legacy that persists decades later. Now, scientists have reconstructed that history using DNA recovered from museum specimens, some collected more than 200 years ago. pages.text: The Humble History of the Bedpan Skip to main content The story of the bedpan is about love and hate, germs and illness, dignity and shame, and, inherently, urine and feces. Agustin Vai/Getty Images Eric Eakin has a three-bedroom house with more than 250 bathrooms. There’s a white one with a tiny Richard Nixon head inside it. Another is decorated in colorful earth tones and adorned with feathers. One resembles a ukulele, complete with a neck, headstock and three steel-wire strings. In the basement of his family’s Bay Village, Ohio, home, more than 250 bedpans—containers used to collect urine or feces by those confined to a bed—are nestled together in stacks, piled on the floor and lined up on makeshift shelves fashioned from concrete blocks and slabs of wood. Eakin’s collection, believed to be the world’s largest, has appeared on MTV and in Ripley’s Believe It or Not! “I don’t think I pissed away my savings. My collection is worth a lot of money,” says Eakin. “You know why? … Because I got in at the bottom.” Eric Eakin has more than 250 bedpans in the basement of his Bay Village, Ohio home. Eric Eakin Surprisingly, Eakin isn’t alone. On August 10, 1988, the Country Today , a newspaper based in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, profiled Edith Martell, who displayed some 60 bedpans in an old henhouse on her property. Her favorite was painted with a chipmunk splashing beneath a waterfall. In nearby La Crosse, Wisconsin, Earl Lord , a retired electrician, once amassed more than 200 bedpans.
